evidence.experimental_conditions: 20% ω-pentadecalactone in EtOH/DEP (1:1), 50 µl, occlusive patch (HAL chambers), 9 induction applications, 10–14 day rest, 48 h challenge occlusion
evidence.support_text: In a repeated patch test with 50 subjects and 11 out of 50 designated as atopics with sensitive skin, ω-pentadecalactone was administered as a solution of 20% in ethanol:diethyl phthalate (EtOH/DEP, 1:1). A total of 9 occlusive cutaneous test plaster applications were given to each patient. By the third week, three slight and three moderate reactions of erythema were reported during the induction phase. After a 10–14 day rest period, a challenge patch was applied; reactions were scored at 48, 72, and 96 h after application. One slight and one moderate reaction of erythema were documented in the challenge phase. Skin irritation was observed in 11 of the 50 volunteers. One volunteer (not atopic) showed symptoms that may have been indicative of a sensitization reaction.

In the data matrix table, benzyl alcohol is reported to have a positive human patch test for skin sensitization.
Positive patch tests to cinnamic alcohol involved 12% of spice factory workers, indicating skin sensitization to cinnamic alcohol.
Trans-cinnamic alcohol is also a skin sensitiser in humans, though significantly weaker, as indicated by clinical patch testing (Johansen et al., 1996a,b).

evidence.support_text: The challenge application caused a positive response to 25% v/v Phytantriol in 8 (40%) of the 20 test guinea pigs at the 24- and/or 48-h periods. None of the control animals reacted to the 25% v/v Phytantriol challenge. The authors considered Phytantriol a moderate sensitizer in the guinea pig.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Guinea pig, modified testing technique, threshold for induction and challenge = 10 ppm.
evidence.support_text: Quinophthalone was found to be a strong sensitizer in guinea pigs by means of a modified testing technique, and its threshold concentration for induction and challenge was 10 ppm.

evidence.assay_type: Guinea pig sensitization test (multiple methods including GLP)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Species: Pirbright-Hartley guinea pigs (various strains). Concentration: up to 10% TCS in petrolatum. Adjuvant and non-adjuvant protocols included.
evidence.support_text: Adjuvant and non-adjuvant four studies in guinea pigs, which included a GLP study, reported no evidence of sensitization in response to a relatively high concentration of TCS (up to 10% in petrolatum) (61–64).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10 male guinea pigs; induction: 0.5 mL 10% AMP occlusive patch, later reduced to 5% due to irritation, total of 10 applications; challenge: 0.5 mL 2.5% and 5% AMP; scoring at 24 and 48 hours.
evidence.support_text: Aminomethyl propanol (AMP) was tested in a guinea pig sensitization study. The test group received topical induction with 0.5 mL of 10% AMP solution under occlusive patch, later reduced to 5% due to mild irritation, for a total of 10 applications. After a 2-week rest, challenge patches with 2.5% and 5% AMP were applied to virgin sites. At 24 and 48 hours post-challenge, the test group showed no observable skin reactions. The positive control (DNCB) induced reactions, and the negative control (saline) had minimal reactions. The authors concluded that AMP was nonsensitizing under these conditions.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Challenge with petrolatum vehicle; Induction: Group I (3.3% GMA), Group II (20% gum rosin), Group III (petrolatum); occlusion; reading at 72 h; female Dunkin-Hartley guinea pigs.
evidence.support_text: Neither GTA nor petrolatum induced sensitization in either of the three groups, establishing petrolatum as a negative control.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Challenge: 8.3% GTA in petrolatum; Induction: Group I (3.3% GMA), Group II (20% gum rosin), Group III (petrolatum); occlusion; reading at 72 h; female Dunkin-Hartley guinea pigs.
evidence.support_text: Neither GTA nor petrolatum induced sensitization in either of the three groups, confirming GTA is nonallergenic in this guinea pig model.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Guinea pig (Cavia porcellus); 50% Sodium Sulfate in PEG 300; occlusive patches (3×3 cm², 0.2 mL) on left flank for 24 hours; induction phase followed by 2-week nontreatment; challenge on day 22
evidence.support_text: The challenge was performed on test and control group guinea pigs on test day 22, following a 2-week nontreatment period after the completion of the induction phase. Two 24-hour occlusive patches (3×3 cm²) with 0.2 mL of 50% Sodium Sulfate in PEG 300 were placed on the left flank. Results indicated no toxic signs or local skin effects in the surviving guinea pigs of the control or test group. Concluding remarks were that Sodium Sulfate was not classified as a skin sensitizer (in accordance with Regulation EC No. 1272/2008).

evidence.support_text: In group I, GMA induced sensitization at concentrations of 0.37% (1 of 14 animals), 1.1% (4 of 14, p < .05), and 3.3% (6 of 14, p < .01). This indicates GMA is a sensitizer when used for both induction and challenge.

evidence.support_text: The human data for citral include a LOEL (induction) of 3876 µg/cm², derived from either HRIPT or HMT.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 55 healthy participants; concentrations 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100% in distilled water; dose 0.1 mL/cm²; induction and challenge phases; 80% concentration used for induction applications 2-4, then 100% for subsequent applications.
evidence.support_text: Predictive testing in 55 healthy participants with PEG-20 methyl glucose sesquistearate at concentrations of 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% (undiluted) in distilled water (0.1 mL/cm²) over induction and challenge phases did not cause primary skin irritation or sensitization. No challenge reactions were observed.

review_policy.eligible_subject: unique measurement-producing subject, donor, or cell-system species
